title: Token-density-driven kernel prioritization for mixed-MIG clusters
creator: Ava Patel
description: Problem: When serving mixed workloads on MIG-partitioned H100 and L40S hosts we observe a bimodal distribution of requests: short, latency-sensitive decodes and long prefill-heavy requests. The runtime currently chooses kernels primarily by model and sequence length heuristics which leads to suboptimal choices for token-dense requests that stress KV memory and memory-bound kernels on specific MIG slices. This ticket implements a token-density-driven kernel prioritization and scheduling layer that: 1) computes a lightweight token-density score at request admission (tokens / expected active KV size), 2) uses score + MIG slice profile (available memory, current freq governor, and recent thermal events) to select kernel variant (latency-optimized, memory-optimized, or balanced), and 3) schedules prefill work preferentially on slices with spare memory bandwidth and smoother clock histories to reduce oscillatory clock scaling. Goals: reduce tail latency for latency-sensitive decodes, lower prefill stall rate on memory-constrained MIG slices, and reduce frequency oscillation due to rapid kernel switching.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime chooses alternative kernel variant for >=80% of token-density-high requests in controlled benchmark (token_density > threshold)
Tail P95 decode latency for short requests improves by >=10% on mixed workload tests on H100 MIG partitions
Prefill stall rate (prefill queue wait > 50ms) decreases by >=30% on L40S heterogeneous clusters under representative load
No regressions (>5%) in average throughput for long-batch requests compared to baseline
New kernel selection logic gated behind runtime flag and feature-flagged rollout via console
implementation_notes: Add token_density field to request admission API: token_density = request.tokens / max(1, estimated_kv_bytes / avg_token_bytes)
Extend slice profiler to track: recent_clock_changes (window=60s), avg_memory_bandwidth_util, kv_cache_hit_rate
Kernel catalog to expose priorities: "latency", "memory", "balanced" with metadata about memory footprint and expected decode CPU/GPU cycles
Scheduler: two-step decision - (A) pick preferred kernel variant by scoring function, (B) pick target MIG slice by scoring slices on available memory margin, clock stability, and current queue length
Clock smoothing policy: if slice.recent_clock_changes > 3 in 60s, penalize scheduling that would increase clock by >5% to avoid thermal oscillation
Fall-back policy: if selected kernel not supported on chosen slice, try next-best kernel; if none available, fall-back to baseline kernel with telemetry event
Add telemetry: kernel_variant_inferred, token_density, chosen_slice_id, clock_at_admission, decision_latency_ms
Expose runtime flag: runtime.experimental.token_density_routing (default off) and console rollout toggle per-customer
testing_plan: Unit tests for token_density calculation and scoring function (edge cases: zero estimated_kv_bytes)
Synthetic benchmark: mixed workload generator (80% short decode <64 tokens, 20% prefill-heavy >4k tokens) against H100 MIG and L40S nodes using our perf harness
A/B canary in staging: route 5% traffic to feature flag, collect P50/P95/P99 latency and prefill queue waits for 48h
Chaos test: induce thermal pressure on one MIG slice (synthetic load) to verify clock smoothing avoids oscillations and scheduler migrates prefill to other slices
Cost regression: ensure average token-cost per inference does not increase >3% in canary
rollout_plan: Internal bench -> staging canary (5%) -> customer canary pool (selected tenants) -> global on for dedicated clusters
Enable runtime.experimental.token_density_routing in staging and monitor dashboards for 72h before enabling customer canary
Provide rollback playbook: disable flag, drain prefills on slices, and provide mitigation script to pin kernels
Post-rollout: 2-week observation window with weekly summary to product and SRE

notes: Trade-offs: aggressive routing to latency kernels can increase memory pressure and drive frequency up on hot slices. The scoring function uses a tunable weight to trade latency vs memory headroom.
This feature is designed to be conservative for Dedicated clusters where tenants expect predictable performance; default rollout will be limited and opt-in for dedicated customers.
Follow-ups: data-driven kernel auto-tuning (learn per-model thresholds) and per-customer softness profiles (cost-sensitive vs latency-sensitive)
Estimated savings: back-of-envelope 6-12% reduction in tail-latency related errors and 3-5% unit cost reduction in mixed workloads based on early benchmark
